case_brief.incident_description: Thabo worked for the employer for five years. He was accused of insubordination after refusing to drive a delivery vehicle that he said had faulty brakes. He asked for the instruction to be put in writing. He was told at 08:00 that a disciplinary hearing would take place at 10:00 the same day. He was not allowed to bring a colleague. His direct manager, who had issued the instruction, chaired the hearing. Thabo denied being insubordinate and said he was concerned about safety. He was dismissed immediately after the hearing.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: I refused to drive the truck because the brakes were faulty. My manager said I was insubordinate and then chaired my hearing two hours later. I was not allowed anyone with me and I was fired the same day.
legal_basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act context

weaknesses: Employer may argue refusal of instruction was misconduct

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Mr Thabo Mokoena, in connection with the termination of his employment with Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd on 21 October 2026. Our client has provided us with his account of the events leading up to and surrounding his dismissal and this letter is written on his instruction. Any further correspondence in this matter should be directed to our offices and not to our client directly.

2. This letter is written on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis in a genuine attempt to resolve this matter without recourse to litigation. Nothing in this letter constitutes an admission of fact or law by our client and all of our client's rights are reserved, including the right to refer this matter to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration or the relevant bargaining council without further notice, should a satisfactory resolution not be reached.

3. Our client reports that he was employed by Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd for a period of five years to the date of his dismissal. To the extent that this is not already confirmed on the Employer's records, we invite the Employer to confirm the commencement date and the terms of our client's employment.

4. On 21 October 2026, our client was instructed to drive a delivery vehicle which he states he believed to have faulty brakes. Our client raised this concern and asked that the instruction be confirmed in writing before he carried it out. Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination. At approximately 08:00 that same day our client was informed that a disciplinary hearing would be convened at 10:00, being approximately two hours later. Our client attended the hearing without any representative, having been informed that he would not be permitted to bring a colleague or trade union representative with him. The hearing was chaired by the same manager who had issued the original instruction regarding the vehicle. Our client denied that his conduct amounted to insubordination and explained that his concern was a safety concern relating to the condition of the vehicle. Our client was dismissed immediately following the conclusion of the hearing.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: substantive fairness under section 188(1) of the LRA: Section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 requires that a dismissal be effected for a fair reason and in accordance with a fair procedure before it can be considered fair. The Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 provides the applicable framework at paragraphs 7 to 10 for substantive fairness in misconduct matters. Turning to the substantive fairness of the dismissal, our client disputes that his conduct amounted to insubordination. He states that his refusal was directed at a specific instruction which he understood, reasonably in the circumstances, to present a safety risk, and that he requested written confirmation of the instruction rather than refusing outright to engage with his manager on the issue. This context is directly relevant to whether dismissal was a proportionate sanction for the conduct in question, and to whether the Employer gave due weight to our client's stated safety concern before treating the matter as a dismissible offence.

2. Unfair dismissal: procedural fairness under section 188(1) of the LRA and the Code: The Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 sets out, at paragraph 11, the requirements of a fair procedure in misconduct matters. On the procedural fairness of the dismissal, the record as reported to us discloses several material defects. Our client was given approximately two hours' notice of the hearing, which does not, on the facts available, appear to have afforded him a reasonable opportunity to prepare his response or to secure representation. Our client was not permitted to bring a fellow employee or trade union representative to the hearing, which is a significant departure from the right to representation contemplated under the Code. Further, the hearing was chaired by our client's direct manager, being the same individual who issued the instruction said to have been disobeyed. A chairperson who is closely connected to the underlying incident in this way cannot reasonably be expected to bring an independent mind to the proceedings, and this raises a real concern as to the impartiality of the hearing. Taken together, the short notice, the denial of representation and the compromised independence of the chairperson represent cumulative and material departures from a fair process.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without conceding the correctness of the Employer's position, and in the interests of resolving this matter sensibly and without the need for proceedings before the CCMA, our client proposes the following terms of settlement:

• Payment to our client of an ex gratia sum reflecting compensation calibrated toward the upper to middle end of the cap-relative range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, having regard to the cumulative procedural defects identified above, namely the inadequate notice of the hearing, the denial of representation and the compromised independence of the chairperson, read together with the safety-related context underlying the alleged misconduct

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Payment of accrued but untaken leave pay owed to our client under section 40 of the BCEA

• Confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due in respect of our client's employment are paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund

• Confirmation that UIF contributions have been paid up to date and provision of a completed UI-19 certificate to enable our client to claim unemployment benefits

• Provision of a certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA

• An agreed positive or neutral reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties

• An undertaking by the Employer and its representatives not to disparage our client in any communication, whether internal or external

• Confidentiality as to the terms of this settlement, the negotiations and the underlying dispute, as between the parties and their respective advisers

• Treatment of our client's record as a clean record, with any finding or outcome arising from the disciplinary hearing of 21 October 2026 expunged or treated as withdrawn

• The terms of settlement to be reduced to a formal written settlement agreement, signed by both parties, with all rights reserved pending such signature

Our client's dismissal, on the facts presently available, exposes the Employer to a claim for unfair dismissal before the CCMA, where compensation of up to 12 months' remuneration is available under section 194(1) of the LRA, in addition to the primary remedy of reinstatement under section 193. The cumulative procedural defects identified above, taken together with the safety-related context of the underlying allegation, represent material litigation risk for the Employer and inform the calibration of the settlement proposed. We trust that the Employer will see the commercial benefit in resolving this matter on the terms proposed rather than proceeding to arbitration.

We invite a substantive response to this letter within 7 calendar days of the date of this letter, failing which we are instructed to proceed to refer this matter to the CCMA for conciliation and, if necessary, arbitration, without further notice to the Employer. All of our client's rights in this regard are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: One factual overreach: the draft states that the manager was 'the same individual who issued the instruction said to have been disobeyed' and treats this as the chairperson identity, which is confirmed by the brief (proc_chair: false means chair independence failed, and incident_description confirms this). However, the opening narrative states 'Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination' which is a slight softening/recasting not clearly sourced, and the phrase 'having been informed that he would not be permitted to bring a colleague or trade union representative' asserts a specific prohibition on trade union representation that is not confirmed in the brief (brief only says 'not allowed to bring a colleague'). No union involvement is mentioned in the brief at all.
criteria.required_fix: Remove or qualify the unsupported reference to trade union representation; confine the representation denial to the colleague as per the brief, or flag the union question as a forensic question rather than asserting it as fact.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "he would not be permitted to bring a colleague or trade union representative with him" - trade union representative is not supported by the brief, which only mentions a colleague.

criteria.problem: The draft generally reflects the HIGH merit band and connects procedural defects (notice, representation, chair bias) and safety context to substantive and procedural fairness arguments, and calibrates settlement toward upper-to-middle cap range. However the settlement term language is somewhat generic in its causal link: it lists the defects but does not explicitly tie the specific combination of substantive score 7 and procedural score 9 to a reasoned proportionality statement beyond 'upper to middle end'. This is borderline compliant with the mandatory HIGH-merit specificity check, but is adequately connected and not entirely generic.
criteria.required_fix: Strengthen the settlement paragraph to more explicitly state why procedural defects of this severity (three stacked defects plus safety substantive context) justify upper-range calibration, rather than a generic listing.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "compensation calibrated toward the upper to middle end of the cap-relative range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, having regard to the cumulative procedural defects identified above... read together with the safety-related context"

criteria.problem: Tone is professional, measured, and consistent with counterparty-facing register; restrained formulations are used appropriately. No major breaches of tone rules identified.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "A chairperson who is closely connected to the underlying incident in this way cannot reasonably be expected to bring an independent mind to the proceedings" - measured and not hyperbolic.

criteria.problem: The structure is largely coherent with distinct claim headings and clear progression. However, the background paragraph conflates the factual account and the insubordination characterisation in a slightly confusing way ('Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination' sits oddly mid-chronology rather than as a clean recitation of fact), and the two legal claims (substantive and procedural) could be more clearly demarcated from the background before moving to legal analysis. No case-law citations issue. No duplicated template content observed in the structured body supplied.
criteria.required_fix: Clarify that the insubordination characterisation came from the Employer, not from the client's own understanding, to avoid blurring whose characterisation is whose.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Our client raised this concern and asked that the instruction be confirmed in writing before he carried it out. Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination."

criteria.problem: Settlement terms are clear, in the standing 3A.10 order substantially, response window of 7 calendar days correctly stated and does not exceed the cap. No rand figures. Order mostly follows standing structure though withdrawal of charges/disciplinary outcome clause appears before certificate of service deviates slightly from standard order (clean record should appear later per 3A.10 item 12, which it does, but the order of items 7 (reference) and 8 (non-disparagement) before confidentiality (9) is consistent). Minor: the standing order places 'withdrawal of charges and termination of disciplinary process' (item 10) before 'clean record and expungement' (item 12); draft only includes clean record expungement without a separate 'withdrawal of charges/termination of disciplinary process' clause, which is a minor omission given the matter is already concluded (client was dismissed, not pending charges), so this is a reasonable adaptation.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "We invite a substantive response to this letter within 7 calendar days of the date of this letter"

criteria.problem: Mandatory current-law check failure: the Code citation is given as 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' correctly in the first legal claim paragraph, which is compliant. However, the notice-pay clause fails the mandatory BCEA section 37/38 check: it describes section 37 as creating the entitlement and section 38 as the payment mechanism in a way that is largely correct ('Payment in lieu of the notice period... under section 37 of the BCEA... such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked') - this is actually compliant treatment, not alternative framing. On closer review this passes. However, there is a separate compliance issue: the draft does not explicitly anchor the substantive fairness analysis in LRA section 188(1) before applying the Code in the clearest sequential way - it does cite 188(1) first in the first sentence of the substantive claim, which is compliant. The more serious compliance concern is the unsupported assertion regarding denial of a 'trade union representative' which is not confirmed in the brief, and the subtle recasting of 'Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination' which risks the draft stating a characterisation as if established. Also of note: no Schedule 8 reference appears, no rand figures appear, no duplicate salutation/closing appears in the Part A body supplied. The most material defect is the unsupported trade union representative assertion, which is a fabricated procedural fact not expressly confirmed in the brief, and under the mandatory check on not resolving conflicting/unconfirmed facts without qualification, this must be treated as a factual fabrication requiring correction before the floor can be met.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the unsupported 'trade union representative' assertion or convert to conditional wording ('to the extent a union representative would ordinarily have been permitted...') and confirm via forensic question whether union representation was sought or available.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "he would not be permitted to bring a colleague or trade union representative with him" introduces an unconfirmed fact (trade union representative) as settled fact without conditional language.

what_is_strong: The procedural fairness paragraph is well particularised: it identifies the short notice (two hours), the denial of representation and the chairperson's conflict of interest as three distinct, factually grounded defects rather than asserting unfairness in the abstract.

The substantive fairness paragraph correctly anchors the analysis in section 188(1) of the LRA before applying the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 and engages with the safety context as relevant to proportionality rather than asserting innocence outright.

The settlement terms substantially track the standing 3A.10 order (ex gratia, notice, leave pay, pension/provident, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, clean record, agreement to follow) and avoid rand figures throughout.
The response window is correctly set at 7 calendar days and the reservation of rights is included in the conclusion.
Conditional wording is correctly used for unconfirmed facts in places, for example inviting the Employer to confirm commencement date and employment terms.
what_needs_work: The reference to the client being denied a 'trade union representative' is not supported by the case brief, which mentions only a colleague; this is an unsupported factual addition that must be removed or qualified.
The phrase 'Our client understood this to be characterised as insubordination' blurs whose characterisation this is and should be clarified as the Employer's characterisation, not the client's.

The settlement calibration language, while adequate, could more explicitly tie the specific weight of the three stacked procedural defects plus the safety substantive context to the 'upper to middle' positioning for a HIGH-merit matter.
risks_to_monitor: If the Employer's hearing record shows that a union representative was in fact permitted or that none was requested, the unsupported assertion about trade union representation could undermine the credibility of the whole letter if challenged.

The Employer may argue that refusing a direct instruction, irrespective of the stated safety concern, independently justified disciplinary action, which could be raised as a counter to the settlement positioning.
The 11-day CCMA window remaining means any delay in sending this letter risks the client needing a protective referral regardless of settlement negotiations.

Has a protective CCMA referral already been lodged or diarised given the 11 days remaining in the window?
What is the client's gross monthly remuneration, for calibration of the settlement proposal against the section 194(1) cap?
Is there a disciplinary code or policy applicable to Northstar Logistics that prescribes minimum notice periods for hearings, which would further particularise the procedural defect?

initial_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is factually faithful in its core narrative, correctly cites the 2025 Code, anchors fairness in s188(1), uses a one-way non-disparagement clause and observes the 7-day response window and cap-relative settlement language. However it fails a mandatory current-law check: the BCEA section 37/section 38 notice-pay clause presents the two provisions in a sequential/alternative construction rather than clearly complementary terms, which is an explicit mandatory defect requiring the Drafting Quality floor to be treated as not met. The settlement positioning is also under-calibrated for a HIGH merit band matter, and the combined legal-claims paragraph is dense. These issues are correctable without re-assessing the underlying merits score, but the letter is not yet ready to send and should be redrafted on the identified points before finalisation.
recommended_amendments: Rewrite the notice-pay settlement clause so that sections 37 and 38 of the BCEA are described as operating together (entitlement plus payment mechanism), not as alternative or sequential bases.

Revise the ex gratia compensation clause to explicitly tie the settlement calibration to the specific procedural failures (short notice, denial of representation, biased chair) and the safety-context substantive point, signalling a position toward the higher end of the cap-relative range consistent with the HIGH merit band.
Split the combined substantive/procedural legal claim paragraph into two numbered paragraphs for readability.
Correct the awkward phrasing in the purpose paragraph.
Confirm wording does not overstate who brought the disciplinary charge beyond what the brief confirms (manager issued instruction and chaired hearing).

supervisory_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is well organised, correctly anchors the substantive claim in section 188(1) before the Code, uses the 2025 Code citation correctly, treats BCEA sections 37 and 38 as complementary rather than alternative, and follows the standing settlement clause order with appropriate cap-relative and non-itemised language. However, it introduces an unsupported fact: a denial of a trade union representative that is not confirmed anywhere in the case brief, which only confirms denial of a colleague. This is a fabricated procedural detail on a HIGH-merit matter and triggers the mandatory check against resolving unconfirmed facts without qualification. Combined with a minor ambiguity over whose characterisation of insubordination is being recorded, and a settlement paragraph that could tie risk factors to calibration more explicitly, the draft falls below the 7.5 floor and must be corrected before approval.
recommended_amendments: Remove or qualify the unsupported reference to a 'trade union representative' being denied; confine this to the colleague as confirmed in the brief, or render it conditionally pending confirmation.
Clarify that the insubordination characterisation was the Employer's, not an understanding reached by the client himself, to avoid ambiguity about whose characterisation is being recorded.

Strengthen the causal link in the settlement intro/terms between the specific combination of procedural defects and substantive safety context and the proposed calibration level, to avoid a generic compensation proposal on a HIGH-merit matter.
Re-run the Part A draft through the mandatory current-law and unsupported-fact checks before finalising, given the trade union representation fabrication identified.
